name: Fire cupping

card.summary: Traditional therapy using heated glass cups to create suction on the skin, discussed for skin glow and muscle looseness.
card.note: Leaves circular marks; burns are documented.

quick.overview:
Fire cupping places glass cups on the skin after heating the air inside, so that cooling creates suction that lifts the skin. It comes from traditional Chinese and other medicine and leaves round marks.

Its looks angle is in claims about facial skin, circulation, acne and muscle tension. Reviews describe evidence for any benefit as limited and low quality, and the marks themselves are a visible effect.
quick.how: A practitioner lights a flame briefly in a cup and sets the cup on the skin, sometimes with oil so it can glide. Cups stay on for a short time, and facial or massage versions are discussed in beauty communities.
quick.risks: Round bruise-like marks last days to weeks. Burns, scarring, discoloration and worsening of eczema or psoriasis are documented. Cambodia's health ministry warned in 2016 for people with high blood pressure or heart problems.

lead: Fire cupping is a form of cupping therapy in which a flame heats the air in a glass cup, which is placed on the skin; as the air cools it creates negative pressure that draws the skin and underlying tissue up into the cup.[1][7] Oil may be applied so cups can glide over muscle.[1] People use it for how it makes the body and face feel and look: practitioners and enthusiasts describe looser muscles, a flushed, fresher-looking skin and, in beauty versions on the face, a temporary lift and glow.[8][9]

The therapy has roots in ancient medicine, with Hippocrates and the Chinese writer Ge Hong (281-341 AD) cited in histories, and Chinese hospitals have used it since the 1950s.[1][2] It reached wide Western attention at the 2016 Rio Olympics, when circular marks on the swimmer Michael Phelps and other athletes were widely photographed and explained in press coverage as cupping.[8] Facial cupping with small silicone or glass cups later became a skincare trend on TikTok.[9]

Reviews describe the research as low in quality: systematic reviews report short-term pain relief compared with no treatment, with weaker or non-significant differences against sham cupping or other active treatments.[10][11] No studies were found on fire cupping for facial appearance outcomes. Cupping produces dark round marks from ruptured capillaries, which last days to weeks, and burns are a documented risk of the flame method.[1][7]

chain: Claimed clearer or more relaxed look
angle.text: People use cupping hoping for relaxed muscles and fresher skin. The visible result is circular marks.

paras: Cupping's origin is unclear; Iranian traditional medicine used wet cupping, Roman surgeons used it for bloodletting, and Chinese hospitals have used it since the 1950s [1]. A Chinese-language review covers the history of cupping, and another review discusses dry cupping in musculoskeletal medicine [2][3][4].

In fire cupping, as described by Wikipedia, a cotton ball soaked in alcohol is lit and briefly held in the cup before the cup is set on the skin; sliding or gliding versions use oil so the cup can be moved over muscle.[1] NCCIH describes cups of glass, ceramic, bamboo or plastic, with suction made either by burning a flame in the cup or by attaching a suction device afterwards; wet cupping pierces the skin and dry cupping does not.[7] In Chinese terminology the practice has had many names across history, including horning and fire-cupping, and a 2016 review notes that incorrect information about it was passed down through the centuries.[2][4] Chinese practice also includes flash-fire cupping moved along channels and pricking-cupping combined with needling.[5]

Practitioners claim cupping eases back, neck and shoulder tension, improves circulation and, in some traditions, removes stagnation or toxins; some also claim help with acne and skin conditions.[1] The ESPN account of the Rio coverage described cupping as meant to loosen muscles and tendons and increase blood flow to speed recovery, and noted that many US athletes including swimmers and gymnasts used it.[8]

For appearance, facial-cupping coverage lists a post-facial glow, relaxed jaw muscles, temporary lift, contouring of cheekbones and reduced puffiness, and anecdotal claims of fewer fine lines and more collagen.[9] The Wikipedia article states that evidence for acne benefit is lacking and that critics note a bruise is a blood clot and does not indicate improved flow.[1]

Cupping was part of Olympic coverage in August 2016, when outlets explained the round marks on Michael Phelps's back and shoulders; the swimmer Natalie Coughlin had shared photos of her own session in December 2015, and press compared the attention to marks Gwyneth Paltrow wore on a red carpet.[8] Wikipedia notes that critics including Brad McKay and Steven Novella objected to its promotion at the Olympics, and that Shaquille O'Neal and Ben Shelton have also been seen with cupping marks.[1]

On TikTok, facial cupping trended in 2021; Refinery29 described small silicone or glass cups moved across the face over a facial oil or serum, quoting Ioannis Liakas of Vie Aesthetics on the pressure drawing nutrients to the surface and the facialist Antonia Burrell on a temporary lift.[9]

Wikipedia documents burns, scarring, discoloration and worsening eczema or psoriasis, and says the marks have been mistaken for abuse; risk is described as higher with wet and fire cupping.[1] NCCIH lists lasting discoloration, scars, burns and infections as possible side effects, and rare severe cases such as bleeding inside the skull after scalp cupping and anemia after repeated wet cupping; unsterilised shared equipment can spread bloodborne disease.[7] Cambodia's health ministry warned in 2016 that cupping could be dangerous for people with high blood pressure or heart problems, though it did not ban it.[1]

For facial cupping, Liakas advised against it with rosacea, sensitive skin, active acne, broken skin or recent sunburn, noted that oils can clog pores in breakout-prone people, and said broken capillaries are uncommon but possible, particularly with glass cups.[9]

A 2017 systematic review of 23 randomised trials (2,845 participants, all conducted in China) found cupping and acupuncture had similar pain-relief rates across 12 conditions; the authors rated all included studies as poor in methodological quality and noted that 17 trials did not report adverse events.[10] A 2020 meta-analysis of 18 trials (1,172 patients with chronic pain) reported large short-term pain reductions versus no treatment (standardised mean difference -1.03) but no significant advantage over sham cupping (-0.27) or other active treatments, and adverse events were more frequent than with no treatment.[11] The Wikipedia summary notes low to moderate evidence for musculoskeletal pain, possibly indistinguishable from placebo, and lacking evidence for acne.[1]

Individual small trials include a randomised trial of rolling-needle versus traditional pricking-cupping for cervical spondylosis in 96 patients, and a review of dry cupping in musculoskeletal medicine.[3][5] Case reports describe fire cupping combined with acupuncture in hypothyroidism.[6] A 2025 paper on a microneedle device inspired by fire-cupping suction for psoriasis therapy is a drug-delivery engineering study rather than a cupping trial.[12] No studies found on fire cupping for facial appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: Ge Hong records Chinese use of cupping.[1]
A Chinese-language review traces the history of cupping, including names such as fire-cupping.[2]
Singh and Ernst's Trick or Treatment discusses cupping's evidence.[1]
Natalie Coughlin shares photos of a cupping session.[8]
Phelps's marks draw wide coverage at the Rio Olympics; Cambodia's health ministry issues a warning for people with heart or blood pressure problems.[8][1]
Systematic review of 23 trials compares cupping with acupuncture for pain.[10]
Meta-analysis of 18 chronic-pain trials finds no significant benefit over sham cupping.[11]

lore.intro: Cupping is discussed in beauty and recovery circles as a way to loosen muscle and brighten skin, with the marks treated by some as a sign it is working.[8][9]

claims.claim: Cupping boosts circulation and gives skin a fresh glow.
claims.believers: Facial-cupping enthusiasts report a post-facial flush and say suction draws nutrients to the skin's surface.[9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes critics' view that a cupping bruise is a blood clot, not improved flow; no studies of facial appearance outcomes were found.[1]

claims.claim: Cupping relaxes tight muscles and speeds recovery.
claims.believers: Athletes and practitioners, as in the 2016 Olympic coverage, describe looser muscles and faster recovery.[8]
claims.experts: A 2020 meta-analysis found large short-term pain reductions versus no treatment but no significant difference from sham cupping.[11]

claims.claim: Facial cupping lifts, contours and reduces fine lines.
claims.believers: TikTok users and a facialist describe a temporary lift and anecdotal collagen stimulation.[9]
claims.experts: Dermatologist-type sources quoted by Refinery29 describe the effect as temporary and list cautions; no controlled facial trials are cited.[9]

claims.claim: Cupping helps acne and skin conditions.
claims.believers: Traditional practitioners include acne and skin conditions among indications.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states evidence for acne is lacking; NCCIH says cupping may worsen eczema or psoriasis.[1][7]

claims.claim: The round marks show toxins or stagnation being drawn out.
claims.believers: Proponents describe the marks as removal of stagnant blood or vital energy.[1]
claims.experts: Critics quoted by Wikipedia note the marks are bruises from ruptured capillaries.[1]

claims.believers: Practitioners describe it as generally safe when trained hands do it.[1]
claims.experts: NCCIH lists burns, scars, discoloration and infection; fire and wet cupping carry higher risk.[7][1]
